steps.user_message: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Atlanta GA. W-2 from Coastal Manufacturing: $96,500. Additional income: $16,300 (photography, 3 clients), $2,100 from Capital One 360, $670 from Merrill Edge. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 720 sq ft. Deductions: $3,200 student loan interest (Nelnet, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have receipt; $1,050 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Below I’ll walk through what looks deductible, whether you’ll likely itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, what tax forms you’ll need, and next steps/questions. I’ll show approximate calculations and assumptions so you can see how I arrived at recommendations. I’m not a CPA — consider a tax preparer if you want exact calculations or have unusual facts.

Big-picture summary
- Treat your photography income as self-employment (Schedule C). That lets you deduct ordinary & necessary business expenses (including a home‑office deduction and the $1,050 if those are business expenses).
- Home office: you can use either the simplified method ($5/sq ft) or the actual method (your percentage of rent and other home expenses). With the numbers you gave, the actual method (allocating rent) yields a larger deduction.
- Student loan interest: the deduction is an “above‑the‑line” adjustment up to $2,500 but phases out based on MAGI — with your income level it likely phases out or is reduced. We’ll need a few clarifying items to know for sure.
- Charitable gift ($1,500) is deductible only if you itemize. With the amounts you’ve stated, you will almost certainly be better off taking the federal standard deduction.
- You will owe self‑employment tax on net photography income and must file Schedule SE; you can deduct half of that SE tax as an adjustment to income.
- Forms you’ll likely need: Form 1040, Schedule 1, Schedule C, Schedule SE, Form 8829 (if you use actual home‑office method), Schedule B (for interest income), and Schedule A only if you itemize.

Assumptions I used for the rough calculations below
- W-2 wages: $96,500
- Photography gross income: $16,300
- Interest income: $2,100 (Capital One 360) + $670 (Merrill Edge) = $2,770
- Rent: $1,750/month → $21,000/year
- Home size: 120 sq ft home office / 720 sq ft total → 120/720 = 16.6667% of home
- The $1,050 “unreimbursed expenses” will be treated as business expenses for photography (if instead they are unreimbursed employee expenses from an employer job, they are not deductible on federal returns under current law).
- Student loan interest paid in tax year 2024 = $3,200 (you reported that amount). Only up to $2,500 may be deductible and it phases out at higher incomes.

1) Which items are deductible and where they go
- Photography business expenses (Schedule C): deductible. This includes supplies, advertising, equipment (depreciation rules may apply), mileage, and business portion of home and utilities if you use the actual home‑office method. If the $1,050 expense is a business expense, report it on Schedule C.
- Home office (Schedule C + Form 8829 if using actual method): deductible if you meet the exclusive & regular use tests and it’s your principal place of business (or used to meet clients, or for admin/management). Two methods:
  - Simplified method: $5.00 × 120 sq ft = $600 deduction (no Form 8829).
  - Actual method: allocate 16.6667% of eligible home expenses. Using only the rent number you gave, that is 16.6667% × $21,000 = $3,500. If you have utilities, renter’s insurance, etc., include those and multiply by the percentage. Form 8829 is used for actual method.
- Self‑employment tax (Schedule SE): you will pay SE tax (Social Security + Medicare) on net self‑employment earnings. You can deduct half of the SE tax as an adjustment on Schedule 1 (reduces AGI).
- Student loan interest (Schedule 1, “adjustments to income”): up to $2,500, subject to MAGI phaseouts. You must have actually paid qualifying interest in the tax year. The lender usually issues Form 1098‑E if interest paid > $600.
- Charitable contributions (Schedule A): deductible only if you itemize. You have $1,500 documented to Salvation Army.
- Unreimbursed employee expenses for wage employment: not deductible on federal return for most taxpayers (suspended by TCJA 2018–2025).
- Interest income (Form 1040; Schedule B if > $1,500): report the $2,770 of interest income; because it exceeds $1,500 aggregate, you’ll need Schedule B.

2) Itemize or take the standard deduction?
- 2024 federal standard deduction for single filers (estimate): $14,600. (If you have other deductible items such as mortgage interest, large state & local taxes up to $10K, large medical expenses, etc., tell me and I’ll run numbers more precisely.)
- Your itemizable amounts from the items you gave:
  - Charitable: $1,500
  - Student loan interest is an above‑the‑line deduction (not part of Schedule A), but it may be unavailable or reduced because of income level.
  - You did not list mortgage interest, property tax, or state income tax paid amounts — those would matter for itemizing.
- With only $1,500 in charitable contributions and no other big itemized items shown, itemizing will almost certainly be less than the standard deduction. Therefore: take the federal standard deduction.
- Note: Georgia state taxes have their own rules; Georgia allows either a standard deduction or itemized state deductions. If you have significant state deductions (property tax, GA income tax withheld), state itemizing might make sense — you’ll need to compare GA’s figures separately.

3) Home office — how to treat it and recommended method
- If the 120 sq ft space is used exclusively and regularly for your photography business (or for administrative/management tasks) and is your principal place of business, you can claim a home‑office deduction.
- Two choices:
  - Simplified: easy, $5 × square footage = $600. No Form 8829. No depreciation recapture complication.
  - Actual: prorate rent and allowable home expenses by 16.6667% = $3,500 from rent alone (likely higher if you include utilities, renter’s insurance, etc.). You must file Form 8829. This will give a larger deduction based on the rent figure you provided.
- Recommendation from your numbers: the actual method looks better because 16.67% × $21,000 = $3,500 > $600. Use actual if you have records for rent and utilities and meet the exclusive use requirement.

4) Rough tax‑effect calculations (illustrative)
(These are approximate and depend on whether the $1,050 is a business expense and whether student loan interest is allowed.)

Scenario A — treating $1,050 as photography business expenses and using actual home office:
- Photography net profit: 16,300 - 3,500 (home office) - 1,050 (other business expenses) = 11,750.
- Self‑employment tax ≈ 15.3% × 92.35% × Net = 0.1413 × 11,750 ≈ $1,661. Half SE tax ≈ $830 (above‑the‑line deduction).
- Total income before above‑the‑line: 96,500 + 11,750 + 2,770 = $111,020.
- Subtract half SE tax: ~111,020 - 830 = ~110,190 AGI before student‑loan interest.
- Student loan interest deduction (max $2,500) phases out with higher MAGI; with AGI near $110k you may be above the single‑filer phaseout (likely you will not get the full $2,500).
- Federal itemized deductions look small (charitable $1,500) vs standard deduction (~$14,600) → take standard deduction.

Conclusion: filing federal Form 1040, take standard deduction, file Schedule C, Schedule SE, Form 8829 (actual home office), Schedule B (interest). Student loan interest may be limited or not allowed — need more detail to confirm.

5) Forms you will likely need
- Form 1040 (main return)
- Schedule 1 (Additional income & adjustments) — student loan interest and half of SE tax adjustments go here
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — report photography gross & expenses
- Schedule SE (Self‑Employment Tax) — compute SE tax
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) — if using the actual home office method
- Schedule B — for interest income > $1,500
- Schedule A — only if you decide to itemize (probably not beneficial with the info provided)
- State return (Georgia Form 500 or current GA individual return) — GA has its own standard deduction and rules.

6) Practical next steps / information I need to refine this
Please confirm or provide:
- Were the $1,050 “unreimbursed expenses” actually business expenses for the photography work? If yes, what were they (supplies, travel, equipment)? If they were employee unreimbursed expenses from an employer job, they’re not deductible federally.
- Did you actually pay $3,200 in student loan interest in 2024? (You said “Nelnet, 2018–2021” — that suggests older years; did you pay interest during 2024 or are you reporting interest from prior years?) If you have a Form 1098‑E from Nelnet for 2024, what amount does it show?
- Do you have any mortgage interest, property tax, state income tax paid, or other itemizable expenses not listed?
- Any business asset purchases (camera equipment) in 2024? That affects depreciation/Section 179.
- Do you have withholding that covers some of your tax liability or did you need to make estimated tax payments for the self‑employment income?

Other notes and tax planning tips
- Estimated taxes: because you have SE income, you may owe quarterly estimated taxes in future years so you don’t have large underpayment penalties.
- Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction: you may be eligible for up to a 20% deduction on qualified business income (Form 199A) depending on taxable income and the type of business. With your modest photography profit, you may get some of that deduction — your preparer should check it.
- Keep documentation for your home office (measurements, photos), receipts for charitable gifts, 1098‑E for student loan interest, 1099‑INTs for interest, and all business receipts for the photography work.

If you want, I can:
- Recalculate more precisely if you confirm whether the $1,050 is a business expense and whether the $3,200 student‑interest was paid in 2024 and whether you have other deductions (mortgage interest, property tax, state taxes).
- Draft a checklist of the documents to collect for your tax preparer or for filing yourself.
